title: Cafe Au Go Go: the basement hub of 1960s New York rock beneath Andy Warhol’s theatre

 Credit: Far Out / The Lexington Herald / Gerald A. DeLuca Cafe Au Go Go: the basement hub of 1960s New York rock beneath Andy Warhol’s theatre
 Paulina Subia November 1st, 2026 · 10:00pm GMT Follow us on Google Discover Beneath Garrick Cinema, located at 152 Bleecker Street in the Greenwich Village of lower Manhattan, lay a basement nightclub, Cafe Au Go Go, a near-forgotten staple of rock history that housed some of the genre’s most revolutionary performers during its short-lived tenure.
 The Cafe Au Go Go may have been hidden underneath, but the nightclub predated Garrick Cinema, having opened on February 7th, 1964, about three years prior. The cinema would somewhat eclipse the nightclub once it began its association with none other than Andy Warhol, but beneath the surface, musicians who would sincerely change the course of rock ‘n’ roll were gaining their footing, performing to its small capacity. 
 Though perhaps best remembered in his caricatures of American popular culture, from Marilyn Monroe and Elvis Presley to the Campbell’s soup can, Warhol was also a filmmaker who produced over 600 underground films during his career. He announced his retirement from painting to shift his focus to filmmaking in 1965, and would go on to produce films in both black-and-white and colour, ranging from short films to full feature-length pictures, many featuring visitors to his (in)famous Factory and his ‘superstars’, the actors, musicians, models and overall fixtures of New York bohemia who found themselves cast under his gaze.
 Warhol needed a space to debut his films and came to begin working with the Garrick, a 299-seat theatre which had previously hosted off-Broadway plays and various love shows. While the place was never officially owned by the artist, it became unofficially referred to as the New Andy Warhol Garrick Theatre or Andy Warhol’s Garrick Cinema after his assassination attempt in 1968, made official as he was hospitalised in recovery after the incident. 
 In a strange twist, the first film that he debuted at the venue was 1967’s Bike Boy, a story which follows a motorcyclist and member of the Hell’s Angels, Joe Spencer, as he encounters a cast of Warhol’s superstars, and also features his attempted assassin, Valerie Solanas, in a small role. Alongside showings of Bike Boy was another 1967 film, The Nude Restaurant, starring Warhol superstar Viva; the film was shot in one day at Manhattan’s Mad Hatter Restaurant in October 1967, with different versions depicting various stages of an all-nude cast. 
 While the Garrick became home to Warhol’s world of bizarre underground cinema, Cafe Au Go Go was still kicking away underneath. As one of the fixtures within downtown New York’s nightclub, coffeehouse and independent venue circuit , it was a staple for performers of all kinds, from musicians to comedians. At the time, the head waitress was Cass Elliot, while Linda Eastman (before she was Linda McCartney) was the house photographer. Performers were either touring and so passing through the city, or were local musicians, comedians and the like who established themselves on its stage. 
 Credit: Gerald A. DeLuca One of the earliest established acts was the aptly-named Au Go Go Singers, brought into the fold by owner Howard Solomon from their roles in an off-Broadway show, to rival the Bitter End Singers that resided in the titular Bitter End Cafe located across the street, at 147 Bleecker. From the cast of the Au Go Go Singers, a reunion of the four members of the Bay Singers came about, a group well-known in New York and Boston. 
 They eventually enlisted a former Au Go Go Singer to join them on the road, before renaming themselves The Company in the form of Stephen Stills . Their tour took them to Canada, where they would meet Neil Young (still performing with The Squires, who were opening for The Company). Under a year after The Company’s split, Buffalo Springfield formed in its wake. 
 Cafe Au Go Go would also boast as the first New York venue to host none other than the Grateful Dead. The band had played for free at the outdoor Tompkins Square Park on June 1st, 1967, but would follow with an 11-day residency that commenced that very night, until June 11th. The residency marked one of the earliest instances of California’s psychedelic rock, coming out of San Francisco, being introduced to the East Coast for a merging of countercultural ideas.
 Jimi Hendrix would find his way to the cafe after years spent recording and gigging around the city. He had moved from Nashville, Tennessee, to Harlem in 1966 and took up a residency of his own at Cafe What? on MacDougal Street, just a four-minute walk from Au Go Go. He formed his own band, Jimmy James and The Blue Flames (he was not known as Jimi Hendrix, just yet), and took himself and his bandmates performing across New York. One of their final gigs occurred at Cafe Au Go Go, playing as the backing band for John Hammond. 
 Plenty of other now-legendary musicians called the cafe home for a night: Howlin’ Wolf, Muddy Waters, Tim Buckley, Joni Mitchell, The Stone Poneys (featuring Linda Ronstadt), Van Morrison, Jefferson Airplane and countless more. Jazz artists, from Bill Evans to Stan Getz, also performed on its stage, as did comedians including Lenny Bruce and George Carlin. 
 Sadly, like many of the other cultural hubs of downtown New York from this distinct era, Cafe Au Go Go’s life was relatively short: in October 1969, after having changed its ownership to Moses Baruch, the nightclub closed its doors for good, and by the 1970s, the building was entirely demolished. Both Cafe Au Go Go and Garrick Cinema were erased, saluted with a gala performance that included Stephen Stills returning to its stage.
